target.title: fix(ui): cap sidebar child sessions with show-more, drop Subagent prefix in tree
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two child-session (subagent) issues in the sidebar tree, continuing the quiet-sidebar series (#110448/#110459/#110470/#110524):
1. A parent with many subagents dumps its full child list into the sidebar — potentially dozens of rows.
2. Every child row carried the hardcoded "Subagent:" prefix (`session-display.ts` prepends it), which is redundant under an indented child row and truncates the actual title ("Subagent: Reading rec…").

## Why This Change Was Made

Maintainer request: show at most 4 children with a muted "Show {count} more" affordance, and drop the prefix where the hierarchy is already visible.

## User Impact

- Expanded parents show the first 4 children plus a gray "Show N more" row; clicking reveals the full list for that parent. Collapsing the parent's children resets the cap. Works per level for nested trees.
- The cap never hides what matters: the active session's branch (`visuallyActive`/`containsActiveDescendant`) and any branch with live runs (`hasActiveRun`/`status running`/transitive `runningChildCount`) always render, even past the cap.
- Child rows in the tree render their real title without "Subagent:"; flat surfaces (palette, search, chat header) keep the prefix via the default of the new `includeSubagentPrefix` option. Untitled subagents keep the "Subagent:" fallback rather than rendering an empty row.
- One new i18n key `sessionsView.showMoreChildren` (English source; locales are bot-generated).

![child row without prefix](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/quiet-sidebar/child-noprefix.png)

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/components/app-sidebar.test.ts` — 109 pass, including new cases: 6-child parent shows 4 + "Show 2 more"; reveal-all; collapse-reset; unprefixed child labels; and a quiet child past the cap with a running grandchild stays visible ("Show 1 more").
- `ui/src/lib/session-display.test.ts` — 11 pass (prefix default, opt-out, fallback).
- Live-verified in the mock harness: child row reads "Reading receipts" (screenshot above; fixture has one child, so cap behavior is proven by tests).
- Codex autoreview (gpt-5.6-sol), three rounds: round 1 found the cap could hide the active session's branch — fixed; round 2 found nested running descendants could hide behind the cap — fixed via transitive runningChildCount; round 3's remaining claim (base-class TS2339) was verified false: the list element inherits from the navigation element (List → Menus → Groups → Mutations → Navigation), the same relationship existing `isSessionChildrenExpanded` calls use.

target.title: refactor(canvas): promote inline-widget hosting and show_widget to core
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Inline widget hosting (`show_widget`, canvas documents, HTTP serving) lived in the `canvas` plugin, but it is de-facto core surface: native apps resolve it via `pluginSurfaceUrls["canvas"]`, and the upcoming core session-dashboard feature (design: `docs/web/dashboard-architecture.md` on the removal branch) builds directly on it. Core cannot depend on plugin internals, so the hosting half moves to core.

## Why This Change Was Made

Zero-behavior-change promotion: document store/pruning, byte-stable HTML/SVG wrapper, CSP-sandboxed serving, and the `show_widget` tool become `src/canvas/*`; the plugin keeps the node-canvas control tool, A2UI surfaces, WS live reload, service/CLI. Groundwork for boards (T2 of the dashboard program).

## User Impact

None intended. Tool name/schema/result shape, `/__openclaw__/canvas` paths, on-disk layout, client-cap gating (`inline-widgets`), Discord ownership of its `show_widget` variant, and native surface advertisement are all preserved (evidence below). Users with a custom `canvas.host.root` get an upgrade-only doctor migration that moves widget documents into core storage atomically.

## Evidence

- Contract cites: URL prefix `src/canvas/constants.ts`; UI constant untouched `ui/src/lib/chat/tool-display.ts:15`; result shape `src/canvas/widget-tool.ts`; discord exclusion `src/agents/openclaw-tools.ts` (commented); core surface advertisement `src/gateway/server.impl.ts`; macOS `GatewayConnection+WidgetSurface.swift:59/74/95`, iOS/shared `GatewayNodeSession.swift:527/666`, Android `GatewaySession.kt:396/432/1171`.
- Byte-stability: wrapped-document fixture (1,558 bytes, sha256 asserted) in `src/canvas/widget-tool.test.ts`.
- Tests: canvas core + remaining plugin suites 223 passed; tool registration/client-caps 118; Discord Activities 17; gateway capability/media 102; migration suite 4. Post-rebase rerun of canvas + registration suites: 4 shards green.
- Size: +887/−595 total; net +136 prod (migration + tests account for most growth; pure move is net +8 prod).
- Autoreview clean (final round after migration hardening).

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) through cron finalization. `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"` and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`, so operator runs record the outcome only (never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot, never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state), while `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming and owning scheduler state — preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550.

`origin` is kept strictly internal. It is **not** part of the public `CronServiceRunOptions`: exposing it there would let any in-process facade caller (plugin SDK, RPC handlers, tests) request `watcher-terminal` semantics and delete one-shots or mutate scheduler-owned counters/backoff/timing. Instead, the public `run` is always operator semantics, and the gateway on-exit watcher — the only legitimate non-operator caller, which already holds the concrete `CronService` instance — uses a concrete-only `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` entry (absent from `CronServiceContract` / `GatewayCronServiceContract`) to get consuming behavior. The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun`) also forwards the true caller origin instead of hard-coding `operator`, so an invalid watcher-terminal run keeps scheduler-owned semantics.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no regression for the #104550 contract).
- The scheduler-consuming origin is no longer reachable through the public cron API, so plugins/RPC/tests cannot accidentally (or intentionally) delete one-shots or mutate scheduler state via `run`.

## Evidence

Real-setup proof at the current head using a **real running OpenClaw gateway process and the real `openclaw cron` CLI** (not a vitest/function harness). Built from this head and run inside a `node:24-bookworm` container (container node v24.18.0; the repo engines floor is 24.15.0), against a real on-disk cron store (sqlite).

```
Head: c071ce7ca34e7a41e4fafab4a8863960fb9403c7
Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.7.2 (c071ce7)   dist/build-info.json commit = c071ce7c...

Built-artifact fix verification (fix compiled into the running gateway):
  dist/server-cron-*.js contains:
    async runOnExitTerminal(id, payload) { ... }
    run: (jobId, payload) => cron.runOnExitTerminal(jobId, payload)
  'watcher-terminal' occurs only inside runOnExitTerminal; the public run path
  forwards no origin.

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (real `openclaw cron run`)
  $ openclaw cron add "partA-ok-preserve" --at "+2h" --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
    -> id 3c309f88..., nextRunAtMs 1784045230759
  $ openclaw cron run 3c309f88... --wait
    -> {"status":"ok", exitCode 0}          (operator path, success)
  $ openclaw cron get 3c309f88...
    -> job STILL PRESENT, enabled:true, deleteAfterRun:true,
       nextRunAtMs 1784045230759 (UNCHANGED), lastRunWasManual:true,
       no consecutiveErrors / no backoff mutation
  => successful operator run did NOT consume the one-shot, scheduler state intact.

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (real gateway on-exit watcher cycle)
  $ openclaw cron add "partB-onexit-consume" --on-exit "sleep 8; echo ..." \
        --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
  # real gateway watcher armed + spawned the watched process (seen in ps):
  #   bash -lc sleep 8   /   sleep 8
  [cron] cron-exit: watcher armed { jobId: a27c2044... }
  [cron] cron-exit: watched command exited; firing job { exitCode: 0 }
  $ openclaw cron get a27c2044...      -> "cron job not found"
  $ openclaw cron list                 -> only the 2 PART A jobs remain
  $ sqlite3 .../openclaw.sqlite 'select job_id from cron_jobs'  -> 2 rows (no partB)
  => real on-exit watcher-terminal run DID consume/delete the successful one-shot.

OVERALL: PASS — driven end-to-end through a live gateway + operator CLI + real
on-disk store. Operator and watcher-terminal origins are cleanly separated, and
the scheduler-consuming origin is unreachable from the public cron API.
```

Unit/regression coverage at head: the public `CronServiceContract.run` preserves a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot (operator semantics, no scheduler-state mutation) even though it can no longer request another origin, `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` still consumes a successful on-exit one-shot, and invalid watcher-terminal runs keep scheduler-owned semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

Persisted-state coverage for `lastRunWasManual` (`timer.backoff-config-readback.test.ts`, real on-disk sqlite store): a **fresh store** where a manual/operator error run persists `lastRunWasManual: true`, reloads from sqlite, and keeps the natural next-run slot (no backoff floor, `consecutiveErrors` untouched) so the scheduled fire still triggers on a fresh service state; and an **upgraded store** whose persisted job predates the field (no `lastRunWasManual` on disk) — on reload the absent field is treated as a scheduled run, so the error backoff window still applies and the past-due slot is correctly suppressed. This proves the new optional field degrades safely for both new and pre-existing stores.

### Proof equivalence: transcript head → current head

The live-setup transcript above was captured at `c071ce7c`. The branch head has since been rebased onto newer `main` (current head `c42041b0`). Scoped to the cron runtime surface exercised by the transcript (`src/cron/service/`, `src/gateway/server-cron.ts`), the full non-test delta between `c071ce7c` and the current head is:

- **`export`-keyword removals on now-module-local symbols** — `onTimer`, `executeJobCore` (`timer.ts`); `resetActiveCronTaskRunsForTests`, `CRON_TASK_RUN_SETTLEMENT_TRACKING_MAX_MS` (`active-run-cancellation.ts`); `DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS`, `AGENT_TURN_SAFETY_TIMEOUT_MS` (`timeout-policy.ts`). Values and in-module usage unchanged; no prod file outside each defining module imported them.
- **test-support extraction** — `timer.ts` and `active-run-cancellation.ts` now expose those test-only helpers via a `globalThis` symbol registered inside an `if (process.env.VITEST || process.env.NODE_ENV === "test")` guard, imported by new `*.test-support.ts` modules. This block is a no-op in a production gateway.
- **four appended `/* oxlint-disable max-lines */` directive comments** (`jobs.ts`, `ops.ts`, `timer.ts`, `server-cron.ts`).
- **rebased-in `main` change #104430 ("cap trigger script tool access")** — `mergeCronPayload` and its `toolsAllow` helpers moved out of `jobs.ts` into the new `src/cron/service/payload-merge.ts`, with cross-payload-kind `toolsAllow` marker handling. This is genuine upstream behavior on the `cron.update` payload-merge / trigger-script tool-access surface, disjoint from scheduler counters and one-shot consumption; it arrived through the rebase and is not part of this PR's proof scope.
- **`server-cron.ts` `toolsAllow` type-guard simplification** — the trigger-script call now reads `job.payload.toolsAllow` directly (valid once #104430 lifted `toolsAllow` to a shared `CronPayload` field) instead of gating on `kind === "agentTurn"`. This is on the trigger-script tool-access path, not the `runOnExitTerminal` / delete-after-run wiring.

None of these touch the delete-after-run / origin / backoff / one-shot-consumption / scheduler-state control flow. The `CronRunOrigin` threading, `consumesOneShot` / `ownsSchedulerState` (`origin !== "operator"`), `lastRunWasManual` (`origin === "operator"`), `shouldDelete = wouldDelete && consumesOneShot` in `timer.ts`, the `ops.ts` origin forwarding, and the `runOnExitTerminal` wiring in `server-cron.ts` are unchanged. The recorded operator-preservation and watcher-terminal-consumption behavior therefore holds on the current head. Reviewers can confirm the delta with:

```
git diff c071ce7c c42041b00bec162b9d7851010db37ad1bb56e818 -- src/cron/service/ src/gateway/server-cron.ts
```


### Follow-up fix: manual ok run must not strand the one-shot slot

A further defect on the same origin-threading surface: a **due** `deleteAfterRun` one-shot `at` job that receives an **operator (manual) ok run** keeps its `nextRunAtMs` preserved (operator runs do not consume the one-shot), but `computeJobNextRunAtMs`'s `at`-branch collapsed the pending slot to `undefined` whenever the last run status was `ok`. The next expired-slot maintenance recompute then wiped the slot, stranding the job as a zombie that never fires and never deletes. Existing coverage only exercised `skipped` runs, so the `ok` path was missed.

Fix: the ok-branch collapse in `computeJobNextRunAtMs` is now guarded by `lastRunWasManual !== true`, so only a scheduler-owned (timer) ok run retires the slot; manual/operator ok runs leave the pending scheduled fire intact. This reuses the already-persisted `lastRunWasManual` field, so it is restart-safe with no new state or migration (an absent field on a pre-upgrade store is treated as a scheduled run, preserving prior behavior). A regression test drives a manual ok run on a due deleteAfterRun one-shot through the maintenance recompute and a restart reload (slot preserved both times), then a real scheduled timer tick that fires and deletes it.

target.title: refactor(gateway): remove forward-referenced resolve in createTimeoutRace
target.body:
Closes #106645

## What Problem This Solves

Removes a brittle code smell in the gateway shutdown path. `createTimeoutRace` in `src/gateway/server-close.ts` scheduled its `setTimeout` before declaring the promise's `resolve`, relying on a `let resolve!` non-null assertion and a forward reference from the timer callback to a variable assigned further down. It worked only because the Promise executor happens to run synchronously, so the pattern was one refactor away from a latent "resolve is not a function" bug.

## Why This Change Was Made

The timer is now created inside the Promise executor, where `resolve` is already in scope, so the non-null assertion and the forward reference both go away. Behavior is identical: the promise still resolves with `onTimeout()` after `timeoutMs`, the timer is still `unref()`-ed so it does not keep the process alive, and `clear()` still cancels a pending timer. The redundant `clearTimeout` that the fired callback used to call on itself is dropped (a fired timer needs no cancellation).

## User Impact

None user-visible — this is an internal refactor of the shutdown/restart timeout helper. It removes a fragile pattern so future edits to the shutdown path are less likely to regress.

## Evidence

**Real gateway runs on this branch** (`openclaw gateway run --dev --port 18999` with an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, macOS, Node 22.22.2), exercising both `createTimeoutRace` outcomes:

1. Graceful SIGTERM shutdown with no connected clients — every timeout race resolves via `clear()`:

Port 18999 confirmed free after exit; the client observed the server-initiated close.

target.title: feat(memory): default cross-conversation recall for personal installs

Related: #99611
Follow-up to #100140.

## What Problem This Solves

Personal-agent installs currently require an explicit opt-in before Active Memory can recall relevant context across conversation boundaries. This compatibility-sensitive default-flip follow-up makes that personal-install behavior available by default while preserving isolation for multi-user-shaped configurations.

## Why This Change Was Made

A single resolver now applies the approved gate: an explicit `rememberAcrossConversations` value always wins; otherwise the setting is on only when global `session.dmScope` is unset or `main` and no route binding has a `session.dmScope` override. ## User Impact

Personal installs receive cross-conversation recall by default. Configurations with global or per-binding DM isolation remain default-off. Explicit true or false remains authoritative.

This is user-visible behavior and should be called out in release notes as the compatibility-sensitive default change following #100140 / #99611. `CHANGELOG.md` is intentionally unchanged in this contributor branch.

target.title: fix(ci): bound docs-sync publish repo git fetch with timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The two `git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main` calls in `.github/workflows/docs-sync-publish.yml` — the stale-source check before the publish commit and the fetch inside the push retry loop — had no timeout bound. A network stall during either fetch could hang the docs publish job indefinitely, the same exposure the merged sibling fixes addressed for the publish-repo `git clone` in this file (#109173) and for `docs-agent.yml` fetches (#110026).

## Why This Change Was Made

Both fetches now run under `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10s 120s`, the exact wrapper shape already merged for this file's clone (#109173), `docs-agent.yml` (#110026), `linux-app-release.yml` (#110027), and `macos-release.yml` (#109174). On a stall the fetch dies after 120s and the existing retry/failure logic takes over: the stale-source check already tolerates a failed fetch (it is an `if` guard), and the push loop retries with backoff and fails the job explicitly after 5 attempts instead of hanging forever.

## Changes

- Wrap both `git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main` invocations with `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10s 120s` (2 lines).

## User Impact

A stalled GitHub network operation can no longer hang the docs publish workflow indefinitely; the job retries within bounded time or fails fast with a clear error.

## Evidence

Exact head: a6b076ffc59e7b172c20c63e945e61861b496c2d.

**Controlled-runtime proof** — a real local git repo whose `origin` is a blackhole TCP server (accepts the connection, never responds), reproducing a stalled Git transport. Publish sync attempt 1 failed; retrying.
```text
Publish sync attempt 2 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 3 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 4 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 5 failed; retrying.
Failed to push publish-repo sync after retries.
[proof] part3: exit=1 elapsed=45s (5 attempts x 3s + backoff 2+4+6+8+10=30s)
[proof] part3 ok: loop exhausted 5 bounded attempts then failed explicitly (no indefinite hang)

[proof] ALL PARTS PASS
```

target.title: feat(ui): merge voice and video talk into one button with in-call camera toggle
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The empty composer showed two round talk buttons: a mic (start voice talk) and a camera (start video talk). The camera glyph collided with the plus-menu's "Take photo" attachment action, and the voice/video mode decision was forced up front — before the call — where it is not reversible without hanging up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Video never rides the WebRTC peer connection in this architecture; camera frames travel only as on-demand `describe_view` snapshots over the data channel. That makes an in-call camera upgrade nearly free, so the mode decision can move into the call where it is reversible:

- One round mic button starts voice talk. The start-video button and its `onToggleRealtimeVideo` plumbing are deleted.
- When the active realtime provider reports `supportsVideoFrames` (via the existing `talk.catalog`), the session requests `capabilities: ["camera-frame"]` up front so `describe_view` is registered — but the camera hardware is NOT acquired at start.
- The in-call HUD gains a camera toggle (shown only for video-capable sessions on transports implementing the new `setVideoEnabled`). Toggling on lazily runs `getUserMedia({video})`, wires the hidden capture element, and shows the local self-preview; toggling off stops video tracks only. Voice is never interrupted.
- `describe_view` with the camera off returns `{ ok: false, error: "camera is off" }` so the model can ask the user to enable it instead of erroring.
- `getUserMedia` denial or camera loss mid-call (unplug, permission revoked — track `ended` listeners) reverts the toggle non-fatally; terminal session errors block and release late-arriving camera streams.
- Gateway-relay fallback: `capabilities` is stripped before `talk.session.create` (its closed schema has no such key — sending it broke relay fallback), and camera capability is reported only after transport construction confirms `setVideoEnabled` support.
- Google Live transport gets the same lazy toggle semantics while keeping its existing bounded continuous-frame upload once enabled.

No gateway/protocol/schema changes; no new config surface.

## User Impact

One talk button instead of two; video becomes an in-call upgrade with a self-preview, matching how the feature actually works (snapshots on model request, no continuous upload). The camera/"Take photo" icon ambiguity in the composer is gone.

## Evidence

- Focused suites green: `realtime-talk-webrtc{,-video}`, `realtime-talk-google-live{,-video}`, `realtime-talk-input`, `realtime-talk`, `chat-realtime`, `chat-composer`, `chat-view`, `chat-composer-redesign.e2e` (100+ tests, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`).
- New coverage: lazy start without camera, toggle acquire/release, camera-off `describe_view`, `getUserMedia` rejection, track-`ended` reacquisition, relay-fallback capability stripping, capability-false on relay transport.
- `pnpm ui:i18n:baseline` clean; non-English locales untouched.
- Autoreview (Codex, gpt-5.6-sol): initial P2 (stale camera state on track end) fixed; final run clean.

target.body:
## Summary
Clear the dead FSWatcher reference after a transient watcher error so usage bar template files can recover on the next access instead of staying stuck at the built-in default forever.

## What Problem This Solves
After a usage bar template file watcher (`src/auto-reply/usage-bar/template.ts`) hits a transient filesystem error, the error handler calls `watcher.close()` but leaves `entry.watcher` pointing to the closed FSWatcher instance. `loadUsageBarTemplate` at line 184 checks `cached.watcher ? undefined : cacheTemplateFile(path)` — a truthy watcher (even a dead one) short-circuits to `undefined`, skipping the re-read path. Once the cached `entry.template` becomes `undefined` (e.g. the file was edited to invalid JSON before the error), the template is **permanently stuck at the built-in default** until the cache entry is evicted — which may never happen on a long-running gateway with a small set of template paths.

**Code evidence**: [template.ts:157-159](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/auto-reply/usage-bar/template.ts#L157-L159)

## Root Cause
- Bug present since the watcher was added in [#98990](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/98990)
- Invariant violated: a closed FSWatcher must not be treated as "still watching." The cache logic at line 184 uses truthiness of `entry.watcher` as the sole signal for whether the file is being watched.
- Trigger: a transient inotify/kqueue watcher error while the cached template is already `undefined` (e.g. the file was just changed to invalid JSON).

## Why This Fix
Set `entry.watcher = undefined` after closing the watcher on error. This makes the cache entry eligible for re-read on the next access, matching the behavior when no watcher was ever created (e.g. the template was invalid on first load and later fixed — the existing test "reloads a path after invalid JSON is fixed" already covers this path). One-line change, no new code paths.

This matches the recovery pattern from [#109682](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109682) (config hot-reload watcher recovery).

## User Impact
- **Before**: After a transient watcher error, if the template file had been edited to invalid JSON, users see the built-in default footer permanently instead of their custom template. Only a gateway restart or cache eviction recovers.
- **After**: The next access that needs a re-read creates a fresh watcher and picks up the current file content.

## Evidence
- **Before**: Watcher error → dead watcher stays truthy → `cached.watcher ? undefined : ...` → never re-reads → stuck at DEFAULT (FAIL)
- **After**: Watcher error → `entry.watcher = undefined` → `cached.watcher ? ... : cacheTemplateFile(path)` → re-reads from disk → recovers (PASS)
- New regression test verifies the full recovery sequence: load valid → write invalid → wait for change → emit error → write valid → load recovers
- `template.watcher-proof.test.ts` confirms 0 watchers leaked

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main, without fix)

```bash
$ git checkout upstream/main -- src/auto-reply/usage-bar/template.ts
$ node --require ./scripts/proof-watcher-patch.cjs --import tsx ./scripts/proof-usage-bar-watcher-error.mjs
Step 1: Load valid template
  PASS: valid template loaded
  watchers captured: 1

Step 2: Write invalid JSON → watcher fires → template=undefined
[usage-template] configured usage template could not be used; using built-in footer
  PASS: invalid template → DEFAULT

Step 3: Inject transient watcher error
  error emitted on captured watcher

Step 4: Write valid JSON and reload
  FAIL: template recovery after watcher error
  Got DEFAULT — dead watcher reference blocks re-read (the bug)

=======================================================
VERDICT: FAIL — 1 failure(s), 2 pass(es)
=======================================================
```

### After (with fix)

```bash
$ git checkout HEAD -- src/auto-reply/usage-bar/template.ts
$ node --require ./scripts/proof-watcher-patch.cjs --import tsx ./scripts/proof-usage-bar-watcher-error.mjs
Step 1: Load valid template
  PASS: valid template loaded
  watchers captured: 1

Step 2: Write invalid JSON → watcher fires → template=undefined
[usage-template] configured usage template could not be used; using built-in footer
  PASS: invalid template → DEFAULT

Step 3: Inject transient watcher error
  error emitted on captured watcher

Step 4: Write valid JSON and reload
  PASS: template recovery after watcher error
  Template: {"segments":[{"text":"CUSTOM-B-RECOVERED"}]}

=======================================================
VERDICT: PASS — template recovers after watcher error
=======================================================
```

## Tests and Validation
- `npx vitest run src/auto-reply/usage-bar/template.test.ts` — 14/14 passed (including new regression test)
- `npx vitest run src/auto-reply/usage-bar/template.watcher-proof.test.ts` — 1/1 passed (0 watchers leaked)
- `git diff --check` clean

target.title: refactor(macos): move PortGuardian state to SQLite
target.body:
Stacked on #110392. Review and merge after that PR.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where the macOS PortGuardian orphan-tunnel ledger remains in a host-global JSON file even though OpenClaw already ships a canonical SQLite table for the same durable records. JSON read/merge/write coordination can lose tunnel ownership during crashes or concurrent app activity, leaving SSH children occupying local ports without a reliable recovery receipt.

## Why This Change Was Made

PortGuardian now uses the existing `macos_port_guardian_records` table in the host-global OpenClaw state database. The logical record shape remains unchanged: `pid`, `port`, `command`, `mode`, and `timestamp`. This is additive at the schema and API boundaries: no table change, schema-version bump, wire-format change, or dual-write path.

The shared Apple SQLite bootstrap/validation code moves into `OpenClawNativeState`, so device identity and PortGuardian compose the same exact canonical version-zero tables before Node expands the database to the full schema.

Legacy `port-guard.json` is a one-time migration input only. Migration snapshots under the shipped Darwin lock, plans process reconciliation outside both the file lock and SQLite transaction, revalidates the exact source, applies a short synchronous transaction, verifies receipts, and retires the JSON file. Runtime then reads and writes SQLite only.

This migration deliberately lives in native runtime, unlike ordinary Doctor-owned state migration. Older shipped macOS writers coordinate through the Darwin file lock and can appear while the app is running. Only the native owner can participate in that lock, apply the Security.framework/CDHash mixed-copy gate, finish asynchronous process inspection before the transaction, then reacquire and revalidate the authoritative source for a short synchronous SQLite commit. Node Doctor cannot safely provide those native coordination or code-signing guarantees.

Mixed-version app copies fail closed. A signed storage-capability marker is accepted only when Security.framework metadata matches the running process kernel CDHash. Tunnel launch holds a guardian reservation from completed legacy reconciliation through process spawn and durable receipt commit; no concurrent store open or migration can enter that unrecorded window.

## User Impact

macOS SSH tunnel ownership and orphan cleanup become transactionally durable across concurrent app instances, PID reuse, crashes, delayed teardown, and legacy migration. Fresh installs no longer create the JSON ledger or lock sidecar.

This is a one-way storage cutover. Downgrading afterward to an older JSON-only app does not expose receipts written only to SQLite; rollback requires restoring a compatible backup or upgrading again.

## Maintainer Decision

Approve both deliberate contracts before merge:

1. The native-runtime migration exception above, bounded to interoperability with the shipped Darwin lock and signed mixed-copy detection.
2. The one-way downgrade/mixed-version contract: old JSON-only copies must not share the migrated state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact rebased head: `0fa751207e10debaba47e22e6840e09d9cf499db`; clean stacked merge onto #110392.
- Developer-ID-signed candidate embedded that exact head and storage marker `2`; released v2026.7.1 was independently signature-valid and had no marker.
- Disposable macOS VM, real signed apps: mixed-version exclusion preserved the legacy ledger and live SSH child without opening the SQLite table; one-time migration retired JSON and preserved one exact receipt; a second launch left it unchanged; SQLite orphan recovery killed the orphan and compare-deleted its receipt.
- Signed-app terminal proof ended `SIGNED_PORTGUARDIAN_PROOF=PASS`. Unified logs showed the legacy-copy gate and `reaped orphaned ssh tunnel (pid 3680, local port 43123)`.
- 47 focused Swift tests passed across `PortGuardianRecordStoreTests`, `LowCoverageHelperTests`, and `RemotePortTunnelTests`, including concurrency, rollback, schema validation, migration races, spawn reservation, PID reuse, and a real orphan process.
- Remote exact-head proof: 87 Node state-database tests and 489 database-first guard tests passed; full changed-surface type, lint, format, boundary, docs, and package gates passed.
- Fresh branch autoreview reported no accepted/actionable findings; patch correct confidence 0.84.
- VM proof was guest-only. The original snapshot was restored and the VM stopped; no host runtime state was touched.

AI assistance was used for implementation and review. Maintainer-directed design, focused tests, exact-head remote validation, and signed native behavior proof were performed before handoff.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-running Gateway processes retained diagnostic references for every completed session, allowing process-local memory use to grow continuously under session churn.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostic run activity now separates session aliases from sequenced active-run ownership, retains completion guards while matching asynchronous events are still queued, and prunes only idle activity with a 30-minute retention and 2,000-entry ceiling. Stuck-session recovery retires only recovered owners while preserving newer work, and run-less reply operations hold explicit activity ownership until their registry lifecycle ends. No public API, configuration, or protocol changes are introduced.

## User Impact

Operators can keep Gateway processes running through high session churn without completed diagnostic activity growing without bound, while current activity remains available to staleness and recovery diagnostics.

## Evidence

- Build coverage: the full `pnpm build` passed before the final test-fixture repair; after rebasing onto current `main`, the official `gatewayWatch` build profile passed at `c627023625f`, including the exact-head runtime bundle, CLI bootstrap guard, runtime postbuild, and build stamps.

## What Problem This Solves

When a user answers No to Proceed with reset? or Proceed with uninstall? in `src/commands/reset.ts:119` and `src/commands/uninstall.ts:173`, the condition `isCancel(ok) || !ok` treats it identically to Ctrl+C cancel, showing Reset cancelled. / Uninstall cancelled. This is misleading the user didnt cancel they explicitly declined.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bug is in the condition itself: isCancel checks for Ctrl+C/Escape (the @clack/prompts cancel symbol), while !ok catches the user clicking No. These are semantically distinct user intents and should produce different messages.

## User Impact

- Before: Answering No shows Reset cancelled. / Uninstall cancelled. despite not being a cancellation
- After: No shows Reset skipped. / Uninstall skipped.; only Ctrl+C/Escape shows cancelled
- Functionally identical: both paths exit(0)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** User No conflated with Cancel in both reset and uninstall confirm prompts
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24, commit `5ea73a1e6` on branch `fix/confirm-no-vs-cancel` (rebased on upstream/main `94e1cc9a4`)
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.commands.config.ts` with a test file that mocks `@clack/prompts.confirm` to return `false` (No) and `Symbol.for("clack:cancel")` (Ctrl+C), then calls BOTH real `resetCommand()` AND real `uninstallCommand()` with a mock runtime. Verifies output messages and exit codes for both commands.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node`/`vitest` runtime verification (copied live output):

  ```text
  stdout | uninstallCommand: shows skipped when user answers No

  stdout | uninstallCommand: shows cancelled when user presses Ctrl+C

  uninstall Cancel: log=[]

  Test Files  1 passed (1)

  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** Real `resetCommand` invocation: No shows "Reset skipped.", Ctrl+C shows "[CANCEL]: Reset cancelled.". Real `uninstallCommand` invocation: No shows "Uninstall skipped.", Ctrl+C shows "[CANCEL]: Uninstall cancelled.". Both paths exit(0) correctly for both commands.

- Config/env/migration behavior: No

target.title: feat(kimi): show code quota in usage status
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Kimi Coding subscription users currently do not see code quota usage in OpenClaw status surfaces. This PR adds Kimi quota reporting to the existing provider usage/status pipeline so `5h` and `7d` windows can be shown instead of omitting Kimi.

This refreshed version also narrows the behavior for compatibility: automatic quota polling now only runs for the official managed Kimi Coding endpoint, and custom proxy/mirror base URLs are skipped by default.

## Why This Change Was Made

The quota payload is provider-specific (`GET https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1/usages`), so the Kimi provider plugin should own:

- auth resolution for existing Kimi credentials
- managed-endpoint gating for compatibility
- HTTP request + payload normalization

Core still only owns provider-id routing, usage aggregation, timeout handling, and status display.

This follows the existing provider-owned usage pattern already used by other providers, while keeping the Kimi implementation narrower in two ways:

- it reuses the existing Kimi auth sources (`KIMI_API_KEY`, `KIMICODE_API_KEY`, config/store resolution) instead of adding a new credential precedence path
- it does **not** assume that arbitrary custom proxies implement Kimi's managed `/usages` contract

The endpoint contract is not speculative: Kimi Code's official implementation also uses the managed usage endpoint in `managed-usage.ts`:

- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-code/blob/main/packages/oauth/src/managed-usage.ts

## User Impact

When OpenClaw has an existing Kimi Coding API key and the configured Kimi base URL resolves to the official managed endpoint (`https://api.kimi.com/coding[/v1]`), OpenClaw status surfaces can show:

- `5h` from the matching five-hour quota window
- `7d` from the top-level usage row

When users configure a custom proxy or mirror base URL for Kimi, OpenClaw now skips automatic quota polling instead of sending a best-effort `/usages` request to an endpoint whose response shape is unknown.

This PR does not change model request routing, model IDs, or auth precedence for normal Kimi model calls.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof was re-run on the refreshed branch head `bbae02b763e` on **July 18, 2026** using the real local Kimi Coding API key stored in the local auth profile `kimi-coding:default` (token redacted), the configured managed base URL `https://api.kimi.com/coding/`, and this branch's `extensions/kimi-coding/usage.ts` implementation.

- called `fetchKimiUsage(token, 10000, fetch, { baseUrl })` against the real Kimi Coding managed endpoint

target.title: fix(plugins): remove incorrect modifying hook timeout fallback in getClaimingHookTimeoutMs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`getClaimingHookTimeoutMs` in `src/plugins/hooks.ts:499-504` is a copy-paste of `getModifyingHookTimeoutMs` but incorrectly kept the `modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook` dictionary as its fallback. Since no claiming-specific timeout dictionary exists, claiming hooks silently inherit timeouts intended for modifying hooks. A claiming hook using `before_agent_reply` would inherit the 3000ms modifying timeout instead of having no timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix removes the erroneous fallback to `modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook`. Only `hook.timeoutMs` (the per-registration timeout) is used for claiming hooks.

## User Impact

- Before: Claiming hooks could inherit timeouts from modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook entries (e.g. before_agent_reply=3000ms)
- After: Claiming hooks only use their own hook.timeoutMs if explicitly set
- Modifying hooks are completely unaffected

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** getClaimingHookTimeoutMs uses modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook as fallback, causing claiming hooks to inherit modifying timeouts
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24, commit `0da592392` on branch `fix/claiming-hook-timeout-dictionary` (rebased on upstream/main `94e1cc9a4`)
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-hook-runner-invoke.mjs` — real OpenClaw `createHookRunner` runtime invocation: creates a mock registry with a `before_agent_reply` claiming hook that delays 500ms (no explicit timeoutMs), then calls `runner.runBeforeAgentReply()` with `modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook.before_agent_reply=50ms`. On buggy code the claiming hook would inherit the 50ms modifying timeout and abort early; on fixed code the hook runs to completion (~500ms).
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (copied live output):


# What Problem This Solves

Follow-up cleanup batch from a fresh audit of the settings restructure (#110445, #110494). It closes the remaining behavior gap and removes drift the redesign left behind:

- **`config.changed` was only broadcast for gateway RPC writes.** Agent `config_set`, CLI, and doctor writes land through the config file watcher's reload path, which never notified connected UIs — so a synced pref changed by the agent didn't propagate live. The duplicate RPC-side broadcasts are deleted.
- **Two chat prefs didn't sync across devices.** `chatPersistCommentary` and `chatFollowUpMode` were browser-local; they are now part of the `ui.prefs` sync surface (schema + types + docs), with `chatFollowUpMode` supporting clearable reset (JSON merge-patch `null` removal). `server-prefs.ts` is rewritten around a descriptor table so adding a synced pref is one entry instead of five hand-written code sites.
- **Users couldn't tell which settings roam.** Synced rows/sections now carry a "Synced across your devices through the gateway." caption (chat prefs, theme, language).
- **Duplicated constants.** Security page's tool-profile list and General's thinking levels now derive from the canonical `PROFILE_OPTIONS` / `BASE_THINKING_LEVELS` sources instead of parallel literals.
- **Dead code/copy from the restructure.** Removed the unused `mode: "model"` branch from the composer model controls, the orphaned `.config-view-toggle` CSS family, the stale "Edit openclaw.json." settings subtitle, "Simple view"/"quick-settings card" doc wording, and a stale e2e describe title.

- **Stale docs.** `docs/cli/openclaw.md`'s config-write policy paragraph predated the narrowed system-agent denylist; it now documents the actual policy (denylist roots, route-backing plugin guard, per-agent routing escalations).

Deliberately skipped: renaming the `quickSettings.*` i18n namespace to match the new page names. It would force retranslation of every key across all locales for zero user-visible change; a comment at the namespace now records that decision.

Maintainer-requested audit sweep ("check everything again… do all of that, PR, land") after landing the settings restructure. The `config.changed` gap was a real P1 for the new cross-device pref sync; the rest keeps the redesign from fossilizing drift.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(agents): avoid synthetic overflow in tool-heavy sessions
target.body:
Closes #107655

Related: #107821

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-lived, tool-heavy sessions could discard a provider-acceptable projected prompt and trigger whole-session compaction when conservative local character estimates reported pressure.

On current `main`, a restored session with twelve 50k-character tool results manufactured a local context overflow before provider submission. Recovery compacted and persistently rewrote the session even though the controlled provider accepted the projected prompt.

## Why This Change Was Made

Generic aggregate, preflight, and tool-loop character pressure now remains prompt-shaping and diagnostic input rather than proof of context overflow. Explicit opt-in mid-turn recovery remains unchanged. When a provider actually rejects context, the existing recovery path records the final provider request identity and prevents resending a byte-identical rejected payload while allowing materially changed retries.

This addresses the common false-positive authority across all three generic gates. #107821 is a useful narrow mitigation for successful aggregate replacement, but it leaves the normal preflight estimator and always-on tool-loop character guard able to manufacture the same overflow without a provider rejection.

No configuration, protocol, provider identity, public API, or persisted-session format changes.

AI-assisted: yes. I traced the runtime and upstream Codex contracts, reviewed every accepted autoreview finding, and understand the implementation and proof.

## User Impact

Tool-heavy sessions can submit their bounded provider prompt without premature compaction or history loss. Genuine provider context rejections still use bounded recovery, and an identical rejected request cannot enter a retry loop.

## Evidence

Deterministic Gateway reproduction on the current-main baseline:

- Accumulated twelve real 50k-character `exec` results under a 1.05M model window.
- Restarted the Gateway with the same model set to 272k, then sent a normal follow-up.
- Baseline made 15 provider calls, triggered synthetic compaction, and retained only 1/12 historical tool results.

Exact final patch on Blacksmith Testbox via Crabbox:

- The same real Gateway restart scenario passed in 14 provider calls.
- All 12/12 historical tool results and the newest sentinel reached the follow-up request.
- The follow-up completed without rerunning tools.

target.title: fix(ci): bound docs-sync publish repo git fetch with timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The two `git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main` calls in `.github/workflows/docs-sync-publish.yml` — the stale-source check before the publish commit and the fetch inside the push retry loop — had no timeout bound. A network stall during either fetch could hang the docs publish job indefinitely, the same exposure the merged sibling fixes addressed for the publish-repo `git clone` in this file (#109173) and for `docs-agent.yml` fetches (#110026).

## Why This Change Was Made

Both fetches now run under `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10s 120s`, the exact wrapper shape already merged for this file's clone (#109173), `docs-agent.yml` (#110026), `linux-app-release.yml` (#110027), and `macos-release.yml` (#109174). On a stall the fetch dies after 120s and the existing retry/failure logic takes over: the stale-source check already tolerates a failed fetch (it is an `if` guard), and the push loop retries with backoff and fails the job explicitly after 5 attempts instead of hanging forever.

## Changes

- Wrap both `git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main` invocations with `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10s 120s` (2 lines).

## User Impact

A stalled GitHub network operation can no longer hang the docs publish workflow indefinitely; the job retries within bounded time or fails fast with a clear error.

## Evidence

Exact head: a6b076ffc59e7b172c20c63e945e61861b496c2d.

**Controlled-runtime proof** — a real local git repo whose `origin` is a blackhole TCP server (accepts the connection, never responds), reproducing a stalled Git transport. The shell shapes under test are copied verbatim from the workflow run blocks; run as a file under `bash` (so `set -euo pipefail` semantics are real).

Part 1 — the exact wrapper terminates a stalled `git fetch` at the 120s bound (exit 124):

```text
=== PART 1: exact wrapper (timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10s 120s) terminates a stalled git fetch ===
[proof] part1: exit=124 elapsed=120s (124 = killed by timeout(1))
[proof] part1 ok: stalled fetch was terminated by the wrapper
```

Part 2 — the stale-source guard (run-block lines 120-122, verbatim shape): a bounded fetch failure skips `skip_stale_source` and the step proceeds down its normal path:

```text
=== PART 2: workflow stale-source guard (run-block lines 120-122, verbatim shape) ===
[proof] part2: fetch failed bounded -> skip_stale_source_called=no, flow continued to commit/push path
[proof] part2 ok: failed fetch skips the stale-source check and the job proceeds down its normal path
```

Part 3 — the push retry loop (run-block lines 128-138, verbatim loop; only the timeout duration compressed 120s→3s to keep the demo short, wrapper flags unchanged): all 5 attempts die at the bound, the loop exhausts, and the step reaches its explicit failure path instead of hanging:

```text
=== PART 3: workflow push retry loop (run-block lines 128-138, verbatim loop; timeout shortened 120s->3s ONLY to compress the demo, wrapper flags unchanged) ===
Publish sync attempt 1 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 2 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 3 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 4 failed; retrying.
Publish sync attempt 5 failed; retrying.
Failed to push publish-repo sync after retries.
[proof] part3: exit=1 elapsed=45s (5 attempts x 3s + backoff 2+4+6+8+10=30s)
[proof] part3 ok: loop exhausted 5 bounded attempts then failed explicitly (no indefinite hang)

[proof] ALL PARTS PASS
```

Merge-base freshness: the most recent upstream change to `.github/workflows/docs-sync-publish.yml` is 64dd2535dcc (#109173), which is an ancestor of this branch's base; the file shape this proof was run against is identical to current `main`.

- Same fix shape as the merged siblings: #109173 (this file's `git clone`), #110026 (`docs-agent.yml` fetches), #110027 (`linux-app-release.yml`), #109174 (`macos-release.yml`) — identical `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10s 120s` wrapper.
- YAML parse verified (`yaml` package): document loads, both fetch sites now carry the wrapper (count = 2).
- `git diff --check` clean.
- Existing workflow assertions pass:

```text

Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

## Intentionally out of scope

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where APNs push and proxy-reachability diagnostics could contain a replacement character when an oversized HTTP/2 response reached the 8192-byte capture limit in the middle of a UTF-8 character.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared APNs response capture now retains bounded raw bytes and decodes them once when the stream ends. Both direct pushes and proxy reachability use that owner, so complete characters are preserved and only an incomplete capped suffix is omitted.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)
target.body:
fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)

## What Problem This Solves

`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` burns all retry attempts within 2 seconds on
rate-limit (429) errors because it uses the same schedule for both transport
failures and provider rate limits. Rate-limit windows are typically 60s; the
old schedule (500ms / 1s / 2s) never clears the window.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three additions to the embedding retry loop, all gated so transport errors
are unchanged:

1. **Rate-limit-specific backoff budget.** When a 429 / quota-exhausted error
   is detected the loop switches to `rateLimitBaseDelayMs` (10s), doubles each
   retry, and caps at `rateLimitMaxDelayMs` (60s). A separate
   `rateLimitMaxAttempts` (5) gives the rate-limit path its own attempt budget
   so transient and rate-limit errors are independently tuned. Transport
   errors stay on the original 3-attempt 500ms-based schedule.

   Production schedule: **10s → 20s → 40s → 60s → 60s** (~190s span, ~3 min).

2. **Structured Retry-After support.** `extractRetryAfterMs` callback reads
   server-specified cooldown from error objects. `postJson` in
   `packages/memory-host-sdk` attaches the `Retry-After` response header as
   `retryAfterSeconds` on HTTP errors. When the server hint exceeds the
   computed backoff it overrides (still capped).

3. **Delay ceiling fix.** `waitForEmbeddingRetry` previously capped all delays
   at the transport ceiling (8s), truncating the rate-limit schedule. Now uses
   the rate-limit cap (60s) when the computed delay already exceeds 8s.

## Evidence

### Gateway + no-header 429 proxy + ollama live trace (Windows)

Gateway configured with `ollama baseUrl → 429 proxy → ollama/nomic-embed-text`.
The proxy returns HTTP 429 with **no Retry-After header** so the retry loop
relies solely on the built-in rate-limit budget. Memory index triggered via
`openclaw memory status --index --agent main`.

Proxy log (4 × real 429, then forwarded):
```
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #1/4 (request #1)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #2/4 (request #2)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #3/4 (request #3)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #4/4 (request #4)
[proxy] → ollama POST /api/embed (request #5)
```

Gateway retry trace (production budget, 5 attempts, ~140s span):
```
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 10376ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 23193ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 47651ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 60000ms
```

Gateway startup confirms updated dist loaded:
```
[plugins] loading memory-core from dist/extensions/memory-core/index.js
[gateway] agent model: ollama/qwen2.5:14b-instruct
[gateway] ready
```

### Vitest (25 tests)

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  25 passed (25)
```

Includes regression coverage:
- Rate-limit schedule clears 60s cooldown window (total wait > 60s)
- Transport errors stay on original 500ms-based budget
- Rate-limit uses separate `rateLimitMaxAttempts` budget (5 vs 3)

### Backoff comparison

| Error type | Before | After |

target.title: fix(agents): report agent-delete cleanup failures instead of silent success
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw agents delete <id>` reported `ok:true` (and printed the removed directory paths) even when it could not actually remove the agent's on-disk state — when the Trash move failed, the agent's `agents/<id>/agent/` state and its `workspace-<id>/` directory were silently left behind. In headless/server environments where Trash is unavailable this happened on every delete: the operator saw success while orphaned state accumulated. A deleted agent id was also left dangling in `agents.defaults.subagents.allowAgents`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Found by the R5 QA campaign (skills/MCP/multi-agent lane, live repro). The delete path used a best-effort trash move that swallowed all failures and returned unconditional success.

## User Impact

`agents delete` now reports honest per-path cleanup outcomes: the response carries `removed: [{path, method}]` and `failed: [{path, reason}]`. The agent is still removed from config (exit 0 — the config mutation is authoritative), but text mode prints a warning for any path that could not be moved to Trash (with the path + reason so the operator can clean it up), and JSON exposes the outcomes. Deleted agent ids are pruned from default and per-agent `subagents.allowAgents`. No behavior change when Trash works.

Design note: this deliberately does NOT hard-delete on Trash failure. An earlier iteration added an `fs.rm` fallback; review surfaced multiple ways an irreversible recursive delete could hit unintended data (user-configured agent dirs, cross-agent overlapping workspaces, retained orphans, create/delete races). Since the reported bug is "stop lying about success," honest reporting is the correct, safe fix — no user data is ever deleted that Trash didn't already move.

## Evidence

- Protocol schema extended with `removed`/`failed` (`packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/agents-models-skills.ts`); CLI handles new + older gateway responses via optional fields.
- Tests cover trash-success (reports removed), trash-failure (reports `failed`, directory left in place, no deletion attempted), source-missing (lstat pre-check → `method:"missing"`), and allowAgents pruning.
- Autoreview (codex gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh): clean — "patch is correct (0.9)". Small, boring diff (agents.ts +47/−18).

target.title: feat(gateway): pre-handshake WebSocket origin gate reusing checkBrowserOrigin
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The gateway's WebSocket upgrade currently admits every connection and only checks the browser `Origin` *after* the HTTP 101 handshake completes. Any client that reaches the upgrade — including a cross-origin browser page or a scripted WebSocket — gets a live socket before origin policy is enforced, and the rejection happens post-handshake. For a gateway that fronts operator control UI and agent sessions, the origin check should run as a pre-handshake gate so an unauthorized origin never completes the upgrade.

This change adds a `verifyClient` hook to the gateway `WebSocketServer` (wired at `server-runtime-state.ts:281`) that runs the **existing** `checkBrowserOrigin` — the same function the post-handshake admission path already uses — *before* the 101 response. No new origin policy is introduced; the pre-handshake and post-handshake paths now share one source of truth (`gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins` / `dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback`).

## Why this change was made

- **Close the pre-auth window.** A disallowed browser origin is rejected with `403` during `verifyClient`, not after the socket opens.
- **Reuse, don't reinvent.** `checkBrowserOrigin` is already the production origin contract; this moves where it runs, not how it decides.
- **No new config keys.** The gate reads existing `gateway.controlUi.*` settings. No `gateway.security.*`, forwarded-header, or `Sec-Fetch-Site` logic is added — keeping the change to a single, proven control.
- **Non-browser clients are unaffected when they send no `Origin`.** CLI / native apps pass through exactly as today; they continue to authenticate post-handshake.

## User Impact

- Operators with `allowedOrigins` set: cross-origin browser pages are now rejected at the handshake instead of after it. Behavior for allowed origins and for CLI/native clients (no `Origin`) is unchanged.
- No config migration, no new settings, no breaking changes to existing deployments *for the no-Origin client path*.

## CSRF note (no regression vs today)

This gate does **not** add a separate `Sec-Fetch-Site` check. A same-origin-only deployment still relies on `allowedOrigins` for cross-site WebSocket defense — which is exactly the contract the post-handshake admission path already enforces today. Moving the check to pre-handshake does not weaken that contract; it only runs it earlier. There is **no regression** versus prior behavior *for the browser/Control-UI/webchat path this gate targets*.

## Compatibility / Scope Decision Needed (reviewer asks)

The pre-handshake gate runs `checkBrowserOrigin` on **every request that carries an `Origin` header**. The current post-handshake admission path (`connect-admission.ts`) scopes origin enforcement to `enforceOriginCheckForAnyClient || isBrowserOperatorUi || isWebchat`, where `enforceOriginCheckForAnyClient` is derived from `hasBrowserOriginHeader`. So today, an **Origin-bearing non-UI / non-webchat client** is only origin-checked under that condition, not unconditionally.

This PR's gate is broader: any Origin-bearing request is checked pre-upgrade. The live proof below shows that a non-UI client sending an `Origin` not in `allowedOrigins` (case 5) and a trusted-proxy-forwarded origin (case 6) are **rejected**. That may change a configured Control UI policy into a broader gateway-client admission requirement for Origin-bearing non-UI clients.

**I am not unilaterally narrowing or broadening this.** Per the review, a gateway/security owner must decide:

> Should `gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins` become a pre-upgrade requirement for **every** Origin-bearing WebSocket client, or remain limited to the current browser/Control-UI/webchat policy scope?

- **Preserve client-aware scope (reviewer-recommended):** keep the existing post-handshake client-aware policy and only add a pre-upgrade gate if an equivalent safe browser-only discriminator is available pre-upgrade.
- **Approve broader origin enforcement:** a gateway/security owner intentionally applies the policy to all Origin-bearing clients, documents the compatibility change, and adds regression coverage for native/custom-scheme and proxy scenarios.

I'll adjust the gate to match the owner's decision. The code change itself is small and contained; the open question is the **enforcement boundary**, which code review cannot safely infer.

Likely owner per review routing: **eleqtrizit** (recent released work on gateway browser-origin enforcement).

## Evidence (current head `4f6e6ccadde`)

Live `verifyClient` execution against the production `createGatewayVerifyClient` at head `4f6e6ccadde` (redacted IPs in `203.0.113.x` / `10.0.0.x` documentation ranges; `127.0.0.1` loopback):

```
1. no Origin (CLI/native app)                         -> 101 ACCEPT
2. allowed Origin (Control UI allowlist)              -> 101 ACCEPT
3. disallowed Origin (cross-site browser)             -> 403 REJECT  origin not allowed
4. literal null Origin (opaque browser origin)        -> 403 REJECT  origin missing or invalid
5. non-UI client w/ Origin not in allowlist          -> 403 REJECT  origin not allowed
6. trusted-proxy forwarded (Origin not in allowlist)  -> 403 REJECT  origin not allowed
7. loopback local client, loopback Origin            -> 101 ACCEPT
```

Cases 5 and 6 are the compatibility-sensitive paths the review asked to document: a non-UI Origin-bearing client and a trusted-proxy-forwarded origin are both rejected by the current gate. Whether that rejection is desired is the scope decision above.

Unit tests: `src/gateway/server/verify-client.test.ts` (4/4 passing). No tokens, endpoints, or secrets; IPs are `127.0.0.1` / `203.0.113.x` / `10.0.0.x` documentation ranges.

## Scope

- `src/gateway/server/verify-client.ts` (new, 57 lines) — `createGatewayVerifyClient`, wired at `server-runtime-state.ts:281`.
- `src/gateway/server/verify-client.test.ts` (new, 4 cases).
- `docs/gateway/security/websocket-origin-gate.md` (new) + link in `docs/gateway/security/index.md`.
- Reuses `checkBrowserOrigin` and `gateway.controlUi.*`. No forwarded-header, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, proxy-header, or `gateway.security.*` logic; no new settings.

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw tui` did not exit on quit. On any quit path (double Ctrl-C, `/quit`, `/exit`, Ctrl-D) it printed `gateway disconnected` then the Node process hung indefinitely (>65s, needed SIGKILL). target.title: fix(ai): keep OpenAI tool call id truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` truncates oversized OpenAI tool call IDs with `id.slice(0, 40)`. When a tool call ID contains a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling positions 39-40, `slice` splits the pair and leaves an unpaired high surrogate — producing **invalid Unicode in the outbound API request**.

## Why This Change Was Made

`String.prototype.slice(0, 40)` operates on UTF-16 code units. A surrogate pair (e.g. 🐱 `\uD83D\uDC31`) consumes 2 code units. ## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where several OpenClaw-owned runtime journals still wrote JSONL files even though current storage policy requires app state and caches to live in SQLite. Those file writers bypassed the shared/per-agent state ownership model and left legacy paths in steady-state runtime code.

The session/transcript store was deliberately excluded because #98236 owns that SQLite flip.

## Why This Change Was Made

The remaining state writers now use the narrowest existing SQLite owner: shared diagnostic events for core audit journals, Memory Core plugin state for memory-host events, and the per-agent database for ACP parent-stream diagnostics. Legacy persistent audit/event files import only through explicit `openclaw doctor --fix` migrations. Core and plugin doctor imports require exclusive state ownership for their full read/import/archive window, preflight SQLite capacity, verify imported rows, sanitize retired sources, and only then archive them. ACP diagnostic files are rebuildable and receive no compatibility importer. There are no runtime fallback readers or dual writes.

target.title: fix(ai): skip blank environment credentials during provider auth
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users could be routed to an unusable blank environment credential instead of a valid fallback. For example, a whitespace-only `ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN` took precedence over a valid `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; blank AWS or Google Vertex markers were also reported as authenticated, and Azure Responses surfaced a generic SDK auth error for a blank key.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared AI environment credential resolver now treats trimmed non-empty values as configured and returns normalized API keys. Provider fallback ordering, auth-status reporting, AWS/Vertex ambient-auth markers, and request-time resolution therefore share one predicate. Azure Responses also uses that canonical result instead of reading the raw environment a second time inside its private client factory.

## User Impact

Users with accidentally blank credential variables can use later valid fallbacks and receive accurate missing-credential status. Valid environment API keys with accidental surrounding whitespace are normalized before reaching provider SDKs.

## Evidence

- Direct production-helper reproduction on Linux / Node 24.18.0 before the fix: with `ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN="   "` and a valid `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `findEnvKeys("anthropic")` returned both variables and `getEnvApiKey("anthropic")` selected the blank OAuth token. A padded OpenAI key was also returned unmodified.
- After the fix, the same production path selects `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, returns the normalized valid fallback, and ignores a blank OpenAI key. An all-blank AWS credential-marker set no longer returns `<authenticated>`.
- The real Azure Responses stream now returns the provider-specific missing-key error before egress for a blank environment key; the previous path surfaced the OpenAI SDK's generic authentication-method error.
- Exact dependency source review: OpenAI 6.45.0 and Anthropic SDK 0.109.1 build authentication headers directly from the supplied key/token and do not own OpenClaw's environment fallback ordering.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/llm/env-api-keys.test.ts packages/ai/src/env-api-keys.browser-bundle.test.ts packages/ai/src/providers/azure-openai-responses.test.ts` — 16 tests passed after rebasing onto current `upstream/main`.
- Mutation check: restoring raw truthiness and Azure's raw-env reread made 4 new assertions fail (Anthropic fallback, AWS marker, Vertex marker, and Azure error behavior).
- `git diff --check` passed.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs -- <touched files>` did not reach repository checks: its all-workspace Testbox delegation stopped during `pnpm install` with `ERR_PNPM_ABORTED_REMOVE_MODULES_DIR_NO_TTY` in the linked worktree.

target.title: fix(qqbot): send quoted media paths with spaces
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QQBot outbound media tags did not recognize quoted self-closing media paths containing spaces, such as `<qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />`.

`normalizeMediaTags()` accepted whitespace-free `file` / `src` / `path` / `url` values, but the same parser stopped matching when the quoted attribute value contained a common local filename with a space. When that happened, `sendText()` left the self-closing tag as ordinary text instead of converting it into a wrapped `<qqmedia>...</qqmedia>` block for the media sender.

The narrow pre-fix trigger was:

```text
<qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />
```

Before this change, that text stayed unchanged and no media upload path was reached.

## Why This Change Was Made

The self-closing QQBot media-tag parser now distinguishes quoted and unquoted attribute values:

- quoted `file` / `src` / `path` / `url` values may contain spaces;
- unquoted values still stop at whitespace.

This keeps the fix inside QQBot's local media-tag normalization boundary and avoids broadly relaxing whitespace parsing. Existing wrapped tags, whitespace-free unquoted self-closing tags, alias resolution, sandbox/root checks, media kind routing, and outbound sender behavior remain unchanged.

## User Impact

QQBot users can send local media files whose quoted paths contain spaces through self-closing media tags produced by a user or model response.

For example, a reply containing `<qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />` now enters the existing QQBot media upload path instead of being delivered as literal text.

## Evidence

Focused parser proof:

```text
input:  <qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo.png" />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo bar.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia file='C:/tmp/foo bar.png' />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo bar.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia alt="upload proof" file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo bar.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia file=C:/tmp/foo bar.png />
output: <qqmedia file=C:/tmp/foo bar.png />
```

The unquoted-with-space case intentionally remains unchanged so the parser does not swallow whitespace that should delimit the attribute value.

User-realistic outbound path covered by test:

```text
user/model QQBot reply text
  -> <qqmedia file=".../tagged report.docx" />
  -> sendText()
  -> normalizeMediaTags()
  -> <qqmedia>.../tagged report.docx</qqmedia>
  -> media tag dispatch
  -> sendMedia()
```

The outbound regression creates a temporary file named `tagged report.docx`, sends it through `sendText()` as a quoted self-closing `<qqmedia file="..." />` tag, and verifies the mocked QQBot media sender receives the resolved local file path.

Live QQBot behavior proof:

```text
OpenClaw 2026.7.2 (PR head)
  -> real QQBot AppID/AppSecret configured locally
  -> QQBot access token obtained
  -> QQBot WebSocket connected
  -> real C2C user sent "proof"
  -> OpenClaw recorded target: default:c2c:<redacted-openid>
```

A one-off local proof script then used the same QQBot `sendText()` path with a real C2C target and a local file whose basename contains a space:

```json
{
  "proof": "qqbot quoted local media path with spaces",
  "targetRedacted": "qqbot:c2c:<redacted>",
  "fileBasename": "tagged report.txt",
  "fileHasSpace": true,
  "inputShape": "<qqmedia file=\"<local path with spaces>\" />",
  "normalizedShape": "<qqmedia><local path with spaces></qqmedia>"
}
```

The real QQBot send returned a platform message id with no error:

```json
{
  "qqbotApiResult": {
    "channel": "qqbot",
    "messageId": "<present>",
    "timestamp": "2026-07-18T16:26:28+08:00",
    "error": null
  }
}
```

Supporting live API logs showed QQBot API `200 OK` responses for the connected account and the redacted C2C openid during the same run. App secret, access token, full openid, `file_info`, and platform message id are not included in the PR body.

<details>
